paras: The attempted lynching of Frank Koehler took place in Union City, Pennsylvania, in May 1888, when a crowd tried to take Koehler, a German baker arrested on suspicion of dynamiting the house of attorney F. H. McClintock, from the officer who held him. Koehler was not taken, and about a week later a crowd of some 500 people surrounded him with threats at his hearing in the town. He was never convicted of the bombing, but in December 1888 he was returned to Sing Sing prison in New York, from which he had escaped in 1873.

McClintock was counsel for the anti-license crusaders in Union City and, according to the Evening Star, had made many enemies as prosecuting attorney in recent criminal cases. He had prosecuted Koehler that February on an indictment for keeping a disorderly house, and a New-York Tribune account said he had also taken up a case against Koehler for killing trout with dynamite in French Creek. In the course of that case McClintock learned that Koehler was a burglar who had escaped from Sing Sing in 1873, and he moved to have him returned to the prison.

At about 2:30 on the morning of Wednesday, May 2, a dynamite bomb made of gas pipe exploded under the front porch of McClintock's house and shattered the front of the building. A second bomb with a lighted fuse that had not burned down was found beneath the bedroom of McClintock, his wife and two children. The town council met at daybreak and offered a $5,000 reward, and Koehler was arrested that evening on suspicion.

The Evening Star reported in a single sentence that "A crowd tried to take him from the officer to lynch him," without giving the time, size of the crowd or how the attempt ended. Koehler admitted that he was the escaped convict but denied the bombing, and he said McClintock had placed the bombs himself to look like a martyr in the cause of law and order.

On May 10 officers brought Kohler, as the wire spelled his name, from the Erie jail to Union City for a hearing. According to the Erie dispatch, "fully 500 people surrounded the prisoner, and a great many angry threats were made." With "the mob so badly excited," Kohler refused bail and begged the officers to take him back to prison, and the dispatch said he was in great dread of violence from the Union City people.

No report of arrests of anyone in either crowd appears in the coverage. Koehler was indicted for the bombing, but the accounts of the result differ: a December telegraph to the New-York Tribune said the district attorney moved to quash the indictment because no evidence connected Koehler with the crime, while a later wire said the jury failed to agree.

Koehler's counsel, Albert B. Osborne of Corry, asked Governor Hill of New York for a pardon in December, presenting a petition signed by three-fourths of the inhabitants of Union City, and McClintock wrote to the governor in protest. Hill refused the pardon, and on December 14 Koehler was handed over at Erie to State Detective James Jackson to finish his sentence at Sing Sing.

The bombing first reached readers as a short Erie wire, run in Ohio, Illinois, Connecticut and Kansas under headlines such as "A Desperate Deed," "Dynamite Is Too Handy" and "More Bombs," that called Koehler "a venomous hater" of McClintock and said nothing of a mob. The attempt to lynch him appears only in the Evening Star of Washington on May 4, which mentioned it in one sentence and passed on to Koehler's criminal past without comment. Later May wires labeled him "Dynamiter Koehler" and "the bomb fiend," stressed the case against him, and printed the May 10 threats in Dakota papers as "A Bomb Fiend."

By December the coverage had turned toward Koehler, with the New-York Tribune's "Pursued by a Bitter Enemy" describing him as a reformed and prosperous baker, though the paper's editorial page urged Hill to receive the plea "with caution." No paper that carried the story discussed the crowd's attempt on Koehler, and none mentioned his race.
